content:
Fatigue is one of the most common and hardest symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and in later life it can be harder to tell apart from other causes of tiredness. It often eases when the RA itself is better controlled, so tell your rheumatology team if it is getting worse. Day to day, what helps most is pacing (spreading tasks out and resting before you are exhausted), regular gentle activity, a steady sleep routine and support with low mood or stress. See a GP if your tiredness is new, has lasted a few weeks without a clear reason, or comes with weight loss, breathlessness, a pounding heart, pale skin or mood changes, because simple blood tests can look for treatable causes such as anaemia or thyroid problems. Never stop or change an RA medicine yourself because of tiredness.

This guide is about one job: living with rheumatoid arthritis fatigue in later life, and knowing when tiredness needs checking rather than just putting up with it. For a general explainer on arthritis fatigue, see managing arthritis fatigue. For a detailed daily planning method, see energy management and pacing.

Why RA fatigue can hit harder in later life

RA fatigue is not ordinary tiredness. The national RA charity NRAS describes it as a level of tiredness that a good night's sleep does not always fix, and it can be worse during a flare. Common reasons it builds up include:

  • The RA itself: active inflammation (more swollen and tender joints) often brings more fatigue
  • Pain and broken sleep: painful joints can wake you when you turn over at night
  • Low mood and stress: they make fatigue heavier, and fatigue makes mood lower
  • Doing less: resting a lot to save energy can slowly weaken muscles, so ordinary jobs cost more
  • Other health conditions and medicines: in later life there are often more of both, and some medicines can add to drowsiness

Recovery after a flare, an infection or a hospital stay can also take longer as we get older. If a bad week has left you weaker, see rebuilding strength after a flare.

Is it RA fatigue or something else? When to get it checked

Do not assume all tiredness is "just the RA". The NHS advises seeing a GP if:

  • you have felt tired for a few weeks and are not sure why
  • tiredness is affecting your daily life
  • you feel tired and have other symptoms, such as weight loss or mood changes, or someone has noticed you gasp, snort or choke in your sleep

A GP may suggest blood tests, for example to look for anaemia (low iron or a low blood count), diabetes or a thyroid problem. These are treatable, and anaemia is something your rheumatology team will also want to know about. Loud snoring with pauses in breathing can be a sign of sleep apnoea: see sleep apnoea and arthritis.

Ask your pharmacist or GP whether any of your medicines could be adding to drowsiness, especially if you have started something new. A medication review is the right place for this. Do not stop or cut down any medicine yourself.

Also tell your rheumatology team. NICE guidance on RA says people should have access to a team that periodically assesses how the disease affects their life, including fatigue, mood, sleep and everyday activities, and an annual review. Fatigue that is getting worse can be a sign the RA needs a treatment review. See RA monitoring in later life.

Your energy envelope: pacing in practice

Think of each day's energy as a fixed budget. Pacing means spending it on purpose rather than all at once. NRAS suggests a fatigue and activity diary to help you spot your own patterns.

  • Plan the week, not just the day. Spread big jobs (shopping, washing, visitors, appointments) across the week instead of stacking them
  • Prioritise. Decide what must be done, what can wait and what someone else could do
  • Break tasks up. Change the bed one side at a time; prepare vegetables sitting down; do one room, not the whole house
  • Rest before you are exhausted, not after. A short planned sit-down is worth more than a long crash later
  • Avoid boom and bust. On a good day, do a little more than usual, not everything you have been putting off
  • Protect what matters to you. Save some energy for a visit, a hobby or a walk you enjoy, not only chores

For step-by-step methods, see how to pace activities properly and pacing housework.

Gentle activity usually helps more than rest alone

It sounds backwards, but regular gentle movement is one of the things NRAS lists as helping fatigue, alongside a healthy diet, relaxation and better control of the RA. Total rest for days on end tends to make muscles weaker and fatigue worse.

  • Start small: a few minutes of movement, two or three times a day
  • Seated exercise counts. See chair-based exercise with RA
  • During a flare, keep a smaller version going and ease off the sore joints rather than stopping completely
  • See exercise for energy for why movement can ease fatigue

NICE says adults with RA should have access to specialist physiotherapy and occupational therapy. An occupational therapist can help you find easier ways to do daily tasks and suggest equipment. Ask your rheumatology team or GP for a referral.

Sleep: small habits that add up

The NHS suggests getting up at the same time every day, only going to bed when you feel sleepy, relaxing for at least an hour before bed, keeping the bedroom dark and quiet, and moving regularly during the day. It also advises avoiding alcohol, tea and coffee in the 6 hours before bed, big meals late at night and screens right before bed, and not napping during the day. If fatigue means you need to rest in the day, try sitting with your feet up rather than sleeping.

If pain wakes you at night, talk to your team about pain relief and RA control. If you have had poor sleep for a long time, ask your GP about cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which the NHS says may be offered face to face or through an online self-help programme. More help: how to sleep better with arthritis.

Mood and fatigue feed each other

Feeling low, worried or stressed makes fatigue heavier, and constant tiredness can make anyone feel low. NICE recommends offering psychological support such as relaxation, stress management and coping skills to help people adjust to living with RA. You can ask your GP, or in England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies.

See depression and arthritis: when to ask for help.

If you are struggling to cope or having thoughts of harming yourself, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or ask for an urgent GP appointment. You can call Samaritans free on 116 123, day or night. If you do not feel you can keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E.

Questions to take to your rheumatology team

  • Could my fatigue mean my RA is not as well controlled as it could be?
  • Should I have blood tests to check for anaemia or anything else?
  • Could any of my medicines be adding to tiredness?
  • Can I see a physiotherapist or occupational therapist about pacing and daily tasks?
  • Is there a fatigue or self-management programme locally?

For help preparing for appointments, see preparing for a rheumatology appointment later in life.

For family and carers

RA fatigue is invisible, so people often misread it as laziness or low motivation. It helps to ask "what would make today easier?" rather than taking over. Help plan the week, offer to do the heaviest job, and leave the person the parts they can still do. See how to help without taking over.

When not to wait

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe difficulty breathing, signs of a stroke, or if someone collapses
  • Get urgent advice (your rheumatology advice line, GP or NHS 111) if you feel suddenly very unwell, have a high temperature, chills or a sore throat while taking RA medicines that affect the immune system, or become newly confused
  • See your GP soon if tiredness keeps getting worse week by week, or comes with weight loss, breathlessness or night sweats
